articles.title: A Socialist Army Marches on Its Stomach
articles.author: Socialist Forum
articles.content: This article first appeared in the spring issue of Washington Socialist . It has been lightly edited . The imperial hegemons are on the march. As Israel and the United States forge ahead with their (paused, for now) futile war of choice in Iran, the ancient Persian country has retaliated asymmetrically by attacking nearby US bases and launching strikes on Gulf-area fossil fuel infrastructure. Combined with Iran’s conditional closure of the Strait of Hormuz — through which 20% of global oil and gas supplies transit — these events have sent oil and gas prices skyrocketing, portending a possible global recession. The world is witnessing a world-historic oil shock that could acutely harm the global working class, especially the poorest among us. This is all due to Israel’s unhinged, insane desire to destabilize Iran, a country roughly four times the size of Iraq that boasts more than 90 million people and a military system built to withstand prolonged conflict. Western capitalists are clutching their pearls like we’ve never seen before. As Isabella Weber and Gregor Semieniuk write in The New Statesman , “one thing is certain: there is a blow coming for the global economy through the supply chain, no matter how soon the war ends,” characterized by “inflation, redistribution shocks, shortages, stagflation and global financial instability .” The authors elaborate how “the far right is the likely winner,” as such effects will by and large strengthen capital at workers’ expense. While oil prices and widespread inflation represent two of the most palpable effects of this conflict, fragile supply chains mean another critical sector will suffer — food. This war is likely to cause almost immediate damage to global agriculture through increasing energy and fertilizer costs as Africa and Asia begin their planting seasons, potentially pushing tens of millions into acute hunger . The illegal, unprovoked war on Iran has thrown several truths into stark relief in dramatic fashion. First, petrochemicals have become an existential weak link for capitalist civilization. Global society metabolizes fossil fuel as its lifeblood. Petrochemicals go into the production of everything from jet fuel and pharmaceuticals to semiconductors, medical imaging, and industrial manufacturing . Much of Europe could freeze without a steady supply of methane gas. Such over-reliance on fossil fuels leaves societies increasingly vulnerable to disruption; all this despite scientists’ years-long global consensus that we need “rapid and far-reaching transitions across all sectors and systems… to achieve deep and sustained emissions reductions and secure a liveable [ sic ] and sustainable future for all .” Source: Canada Energy Regulator The Gulf region and Strait of Hormuz represent a single point of failure for the production not just of oil and gas, but many other commodities such as chemicals — the region is exposing deep fragility in the global capitalist system. As Peter McKillop writes , “fossil fuels aren’t a shield against chaos. They are a conduit for it.” Fossil fuels’ unparalleled profitability make them lightning rods for conflict. Humans and their societies are utterly dependent on fossil fuels to grow, process, transport, and make food. To the world’s misfortune, 58% of synthetic fertilizer production depends on fossil fuels , namely methane (euphemistically misnamed “natural”) gas. As a result of the imperialist war in the Gulf, methane gas production has taken heavy blows, sending the prices for some fertilizers soaring 30–40% . Alarmingly, because the Strait of Hormuz facilitates 30% of global fertilizer trade, the war could endanger two key ingredients in synthetic fertilizer production, ammonia and urea. Reuters reports that “there are no strategic global stockpiles for fertilizers,” so if we lose them, many national food systems could soon be imperiled. It is in the interests of no one but capitalists to have such a key food system input entirely reliant on fossil fuels, a volatile class of commodities at the utmost mercy of geopolitical power plays and dangerous price fluctuations. Socialists must organize against fossil capitalism by working to transform our toxic, industrial, and unjust food system into one that empowers workers and communities around the world to feed themselves while regenerating nature. Mining the Soil, Poisoning Life How is it that a regional war halfway across the world could have such a disproportionate impact on global food systems? Because of humanity’s reliance on industrial agriculture. Industrial agriculture (IA) was the inevitable creation of capitalism, a social system reliant on unlimited physical expansion and a logic of violence against land and labor. The story of how IA arose in the United States is a complex yet vital one for understanding how we got here. According to Johns Hopkins University, during the 20th century, agriculture “ underwent greater change than it had since it was first adopted some 13,000 years ago .” The pillars of this massive change? Specialization, mechanization, chemical inputs, and consolidation and concentration of capital. Before IA gradually dismantled traditional food systems in the US, the typical American farm produced many different products, both animal and plant. But over the last 150 years, farms have become a kind of land factory , with outputs — such as grains, animals, vegetables — and inputs, such as feed, fertilizer, antibiotics, and pesticides . The new logic was actually the same logic capitalists had been using to run factories and exploit workers for decades: maximize efficiency and productivity while minimizing labor and costs. And this new system was inherently dependent on oil for energy and feedstock — it needed coal, oil, and gas to power itself, as well as to create fertilizers and pesticides. Diets changed as emboldened agribusinesses promoted and normalized fake butter substitutes and industrial seed oils to displace traditional fats like coconut oil, lard, suet, and butter. With IA, the landscape changed dramatically, too. Whereas rural areas once boasted diverse “agro-ecosystems” mixing crop and animal production, pastures, and woodlands, we now had monocultures — large, single-crop farms specializing in just one product. These new monoculture-based economies of scale pressured farmers to consolidate into larger and larger operations, crowding out smaller, more biodiverse farms. Our food system further changed for the worse as capital consolidated animal slaughtering and processing operations , leading to a decline in once-abundant local slaughterhouses. If farms became factories, farmworkers became factory workers — and they have traditionally been some of the most vulnerable workers in our society. Both the National Labor Relations Act of 1935 and the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938, two of the US’s cornerstone labor laws, explicitly excluded farmworkers. This gave owners and capitalists the power to exploit the people who keep us alive by growing our food in all imaginable weather conditions, day in and day out. Even though extreme heat has been increasing since 2015, as of 2026, farmworkers still have no federal heat protections in place. Monocultures were central to the so-called Green Revolution (GR), the neoliberal, 1960s project to address hunger by focusing on maximizing efficiency and crop yields through chemical fertilizers and mechanization. As agroecology expert Miguel Altieri details , the GR’s intensification of agriculture may have enhanced crop production — but it also “proved to be unsustainable as it damaged the environment, caused dramatic loss of biodiversity and associated traditional knowledge, favored wealthier farmers, and left many poor farmers deeper in debt.” In many ways, the world is still reeling from the effects of the Green Revolution. IA’s heavy reliance on fossil fuels continues to worsen climate change . Fertilizer use generates the potent greenhouse gas nitrous oxide (N 2 O), and conventional pesticides and herbicides — like neonicotinoids and RoundUp — wreak havoc on human health and decimate bee populations . By organizing food production around monoculture, IA treats land as if it were barren and expendable, when the exact opposite is true. Even worse: in their current form, global food systems fail to meet the world’s dietary needs, with 1 billion people hungry and 2 billion people overweight. Widespread hunger and diabetes-obesity are two of the biggest manifestations of malnutrition, and both stem from the fact that food systems exist to maximize profits, not optimize human diets . From corporate consolidation to malnutrition and the chronic disease epidemic, the modern food system fails to provision human and planetary health, driving instead the deterioration of each. The causes of hunger are complex, including poverty, conflict, and food loss. But there is no excuse for hunger on a planet that produces enough food for 10 billion people . Twenty percent of all food produced goes to waste, amounting to 1 billion meals per day; this equals $1 trillion in total losses to the global economy. Clearly, nothing about the industrial food system is sustainable or desirable. By prioritizing size and efficiency over quality and nutrition per acre, modern farms crank out nutrient-poor foods laden with toxins that harm human health and the environment. Consolidation incentivizes the cheapening of food quality at everyone’s expense. By contrast, creating a food system within planetary boundaries to reverse chronic disease and ecosystem destruction would mean relocalizing food production, making it economical, organic, biodiverse, and as free of toxic inputs as possible. Strong state support will be vital to such food systems transformation toward sustainability and agroecology. Effectively transitioning our food systems away from fossil fuels will harden them against oil price shocks, as well as energy and fertilizer shortages we are very likely to witness as a result of the Iranian war. This is what socialists must organize for — for the good of our farms and the life-support ecosystems that keep earth habitable for us. A Just Transition Must Center Food Systems Transformation The war in Iran is exposing the world’s reliance on the fossil fuels destroying our life-support ecosystems — and making clear the urgent need for a just transition to a green economy. What ecosocialists and others on the Left must contend with is that equitably transitioning the food system is just as urgent as quickly phasing out the fossil fuel industry. They go hand in hand. If we do the latter without the former, we are setting up the food system — and society itself — for collapse as extreme weather intensifies. Remaking our food systems around worker and community control must be core to our project of realizing a socialist society. It is also vital to our work of saving the life-support ecosystems, and earth systems, that our species depends on to survive. Socialists may be unaware that the most important group of climate scientists on Earth, the International Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), has said that land-based solutions — including agriculture, forestry, and ecosystem management, of which agriculture is a key part — “ can not only provide large-scale reductions of emissions but can also remove and store CO 2 at scale ,” including benefits to biodiversity and ecosystems. Soil is the largest land-based system that stores carbon — and the most powerful way to enhance soil carbon storage is through agroecology. Agroecology is the holistic, integrated, and Indigenous-informed science of designing and maintaining sustainable food systems. It’s about food production with nature , rather than against it. Current evidence suggests that fully implemented sustainable agriculture could help offset 10–15% of the world’s annual greenhouse gas emissions. With the Iran war threatening an energy crisis worse than what we saw during COVID-19 , and one based on supply rather than demand disruption, the Left has an opportunity to elevate sustainable food systems to their just priority — not as a strategically optional issue, but rather a central tenet of our movement. A survival imperative. (Indeed, the crisis may already be accelerating the global transition to renewables and electrification. Sam Butler-Sloss of the global energy think tank Ember recently opined, “[high] fossil prices drive switching, making already cheap electrotech even more competitive… With electrotech, nations now have the tools to increasingly eliminate imported fuels altogether .”) We urgently need to bring about a just transition to create a global food system based on food sovereignty and justice, not biopiracy and poor working conditions for farmworkers ; biodiversity, not monoculture; one based on climate resilient, small- and medium-scale farming, not industrial farms. The new food system must use integrated pest management and organic principles to maximize human and planetary health, instead of applying toxic pesticides that cause Parkinson’s Disease , cancer, and other maladies. Instead of a highly unequal, corporate-controlled food system dependent on toxic fossil fuel-based inputs, we must seize the means of food production to create a liberatory food system for all. Justly transforming the world’s food system would empower global South countries with national sovereignty, including food sovereignty, so they could chart their own developmental course and prioritize feeding their populations first. But while we may aspire to global transformation, we must not neglect our responsibility to change local conditions stateside. Where the Left Should Go From Here Internal dynamics on the Left reflect the broader societal tendency to take food systems and food workers for granted. Even on the climate Left, of which I am a part, we have a lamentable tendency to deprioritize — or even dismiss altogether — food systems and rural communities. Yet without them, we couldn’t do socialism. We would starve. Granted, community gardens are modestly popular among Democratic Socialists of America members and in some DSA chapters . However, while useful for mutual aid and community building, they are an incomplete approach to food systems organizing without rural-urban solidarity work like farmworker organizing. Part of the deprioritization I mention above is understandable; the US population, and thus socialist and leftist capacity, is concentrated in urban areas. Socialists in DSA focus on local-level work in their own or adjacent communities by default — which makes sense — and consequently spend most of their time organizing in cities and neighborhoods. But have we been neglecting rural-urban solidarity work to the detriment of the movement? I believe so. I am not the first person on the Left to acknowledge this. I strongly agree with AJ Kohler, who writes , “…in order to form a movement that can beat the capitalist class, socialists and DSA must develop a dedicated rural organizing strategy… Census data indicates that about 20% of the entire population lives in ‘rural’ areas…” At least some socialists have been concerned about this for some time. Several years ago, a Rural, Suburban, and Small City DSA caucus formed to advocate for priorities that benefited smaller chapters at the 2019 DSA National Convention in Atlanta. To my knowledge, that caucus has since dissolved — but the sentiments behind it have not, because DSA has many rural chapters . Ongoing advocacy has resulted in promising developments for smaller and rural chapters. Dues-sharing, wherein chapters receive a cut of the dues payments their members make, has facilitated fairer resourcing for DSA’s urban and rural chapters alike. Recently, the DSA National Political Committee passed a resolution to increase dues shares to chapters significantly through DSA’s 2027 fiscal year, a promising move to create even more equity across less resourced chapters. For my chapter, Metro DC DSA, a strong first step for farmworker organizing would be to get the lay of the land by reaching out to organizations such as the National Sustainable Agriculture Coalition, Virginia Farmworker Advocacy Network, Farmworker Justice, and the legendary United Farm Workers union. These organizations may be well-positioned to consult us on how and where to connect with local farmworkers, in addition to understanding the extent of unionization in local agriculture. From there, DSA members could connect directly with farmworkers in the DMV, learn about their issues and concerns, and solicit ways or potential campaigns for advancing their causes. We can also build stronger urban-rural relationships within DSA. Several years ago, I organized a Regional Solidarity Conference in Northern California to build connections between urban and rural chapters. At the time, I was active in DSA’s East Bay chapter, and Fresno DSA was kind enough to host the conference. The concept was simple: each chapter gave a presentation on its activities, strengths, challenges, and help needed. We were treated to a tour of Fresno, a city in the heart of California’s vast, heavily rural, and agricultural Central Valley — and a city that coastal California routinely dismisses. It was very rewarding to learn from our rural comrades, dance cumbia, and socialize with them. I’m proud to say that that effort led to the strengthening of ties among Central Valley chapters. This is just one example of what is possible when urban chapters intentionally set out to foster ties with their smaller, more rural counterparts. The Democratic Socialists of America has matured and grown tremendously in the past seven years, through several fraught national leadership cohorts and dramatic political crises. Yet we have a long way to go to strengthen rural-urban solidarity on the one hand, and build an effective campaign for sustainable food systems on the other. Socialists should demand a climate-resilient, worker-controlled, planned, and decentralized food system that is not reliant on single points of failure. We should organize for a food system whose core principles are food sovereignty, carbon negativity, ecological regeneration, and food justice. Without food, the global working class would starve, and societies everywhere would collapse in short order. We should no longer take food system workers and the complex ecosystems that allow food to happen for granted. Through farmworker organizing, forging urban-rural solidarity, and advocating for sustainable agriculture policy, we can help evolve the food system from one based on waging war against nature to a system based on food sovereignty, economic justice, climate resilience, and healing the “ metabolic rift .” The socialist movement’s success depends on it.

articles.title: E is for “Exploitation”
articles.author: Rochester Red Star: News from Rochester DSA
articles.content: by Gregory Lebens-Higgins “All surplus-value, whatever particular form (profit, interest, or rent) it may subsequently crystallize into, is in substance the materialization of unpaid labor.” – Marx What does it mean when the socialist movement decries the exploitation of the working class? Defenders of the free market tell us that wage labor is a voluntary exchange of mutual benefit for employer and employee, and allows workers to stay or leave their jobs as they please in search of better pay or working conditions. But for workers, the free market also means exposure to market fluctuations that often result in the loss of wages, hours, or the job itself. In a capitalist economic system, all workers are exploited. We are forced to sell our labor to access the means of life, turning to the market to purchase food, housing, healthcare, and the other necessities of modern life. There is no free real estate available to those who desire to grow all their own food, nor ready access to machines able to produce all the materials of daily comfort. Workers create all value. Capitalists, compelled to expand their wealth, invest capital to purchase raw materials and pay wages. In the process of production, workers turn raw materials into finished goods by applying their labor. These finished goods are sold on the market as commodities. Outside of manufacturing, many modern professions create value in less tangible ways. For example, retail employees provide value to the store they work in by operating cash registers, cleaning, and stocking shelves. This added value, in the form of profit, accumulates to the capitalist. To maximize his profit, the capitalist pays workers as little as possible, and maximizes the use of their labor-power by increasing the hours or intensity of their labor. The worker’s need to recover energy for the next shift by getting some rest presents a natural limit to their exploitation. Further limitations, such as the eight-hour workday, weekends, and the minimum wage, were only won through struggle. The value added by workers far outpaces their wages. For example, if a worker takes two hours to reproduce the value equal to their wages for an entire eight-hour shift, the remaining six hours solely benefit the capitalist. These six hours are alienated from the worker, who has no determination over how this surplus-value is spent. The enriched capitalist, with newfound value at his disposal, has produced none of it. The ratio of surplus-value to remunerated labor defines the rate of exploitation. “The rate of surplus-value depends . . . on the degree of exploitation of labor-power,” says Marx. The higher the rate of exploitation, the more profit that accrues to the capitalist. In the example above, the capitalist has exploited the worker’s labor-power at a rate of 300% (6 hours:2 hours). Despite any advancements in worker’s rights, the deviation between productivity and wages has expanded year over year, demonstrating an increasing rate of exploitation for the working class. Workers continue to be paid at subsistence rates while producing ever more wealth for capitalists. Labor exploitation is not the only form of oppression under capitalism. Capitalists invest in suppressing working-class power by hiring strikebreakers, lobbying politicians, and proselytizing for capitalism. Workers who attempt to organize a force that challenges their rule by capital are often cut down by its bullets. Capital is not hesitant to use violent coercion once economic coercion has failed. The rate of exploitation varies along racialized lines. Race is a tool exploited by the capitalist class to divide workers and to excuse the hyper-exploitation of minorities. Other groups, including women, children, individuals with disabilities, and prisoners, also experience increased exploitation. Despite the exploitation and violence upholding their positions, capitalists may argue they have earned their profit as a reward for the risk of investment. But where did the wealth they invest originate? Their inheritance represents centuries of exploitation accumulated in generational wealth. Much of their capital has its origin in the colonial theft of land and resources, ongoing today. The self-made businessman is a myth. Capitalists further exploit us as consumers. Most of the wages taken home by workers go right back to the capitalist class in the form of rent, gas, utilities, and other expenses. Monopolized corporations charge whatever they can get away with for products, while wage increases continue to fall behind inflated prices. In its never-ending drive for expansion, capitalism seeks the maximization of profit over all other incentives. Capitalism will always trend toward an increase in the rate of exploitation. Any real freedoms experienced by workers have been won through struggle. Exploitation will only cease when workers democratically control our own labor; when we work not for the private accumulation of profit, but for the collective benefit of the whole of society. The post E is for “Exploitation” first appeared on Rochester Red Star .

articles.title: Working-Class Voters Are Winnable for the Left. Here’s How.
articles.author: Ned Rust
articles.content: In a new report from the Equality Action Center, Joan C. Williams and Jared Abbott lay out a sensible, pragmatic approach to what has always seemed a Sisyphean task: explaining to progressives how they can turn more people on to their politics than they turn off. In so doing, Williams and Abbott offer a means to block one of the misanthropic right’s signature moves: playing populist and turning the working class against a college-educated left that wants to address our system’s fundamental injustices.The report is essentially a “For Dummies” coalition guide for progressive smarties (especially social justice advocates, political candidates, and funders) that shows how to recognize and redirect the antisocial, prejudicial habits of their class and channel them toward the common goal of taking populism back from the Right.Much of the guide’s wisdom comes down to the broad working class’s perception that college-educated voters are too focused on problems that don’t affect workers’ lives. Citizens scrabbling just to get by are turned off when they see elites focusing on issues that may be real and significant but that they perceive are at a distance from the pressures they face to put food on the table, collect a paycheck, and pay the rent.Wage-earners certainly are not mostly anti-LGBT, anti-international, anti-immigration, anti-art, anti–gun control, anti-abortion, anti-democracy, or anti-environment. But they do prioritize issues directly connected to their economic and social precarity. This is not hard to understand, and progressive and the Left — if they hope to win the trust of working-class voters — need to remember it.This is exemplified by the biggest priority gap in the survey: the 40-point delta (90 percent versus 50 percent) between liberal college-educated voters and no-four-year-degree working-class voters on “defending democracy.” The issue was the second-highest priority for the college set, but just the nineteenth (of the twenty-five priorities Williams and Abbott tested) for the working class. Food, jobs, health, wages, and safety outpoll any four-syllable word used by a group that’s uphill from you.And what about that darling term of the current election cycle, “affordability”? The buzzword is broken out into its components (jobs, wages, work conditions, consumer costs, etc.). It’s found that the college set is preoccupied with the consumer-costs side of the affordability crisis versus the working class, which prioritizes the predistributive costs associated with jobs, wages, housing, and health care. The working class is accustomed to living without a credit line (or an investment portfolio) buffer, the college set less so. The takeaway: when speaking to affordability, progressive and left candidates need to speak not just to store and restaurant prices but to the mortal impacts of low wages and high rent.Of the issues tested, the three largest gaps where college grads trailed working-class respondents — and in every racial group — concerned personal security. This should not surprise anyone.Do more educated, affluent people inhabit safer, or more dangerous communities? Are there more precariously situated noncitizens in Ypsilanti or Grosse Pointe, Michigan? Are there more in Chappaqua or Mount Vernon, New York? What about Oakland versus Menlo Park, California? Working-class respondents favored securing the border by 28.3 points, lowering the crime rate by 21.8 points, and adding more police by 19.3 points.On the other side, issues that college grads prioritize more than the working class, there are four issues with a wide spread. The college set prefers: LGBTQ+ rights by 32 points, immigration by 32 points, climate by 29 points, and abortion rights by 26 points.These are called “wedge issues,” given their tactical utility to strategists on the Right. It’s not that these issues don’t matter — not even a slim majority of working-class voters wishes to persecute minorities, force women to have unwanted children, or further disrupt the climate. But they are simply not seen as immediate as the threats that come from not paying your rent, car payments, daycare, and medical bills — existential issues that those on the college track don’t experience so often or acutely.Here, Williams and Abbott identify how to find enough common ground on issues to fend off the wedge-driving political operatives on the right.The study doesn’t pretend to test every framing under the sun, but it does get after many, and successfully so. The researchers provide a well-stocked workshop filled with ready-to-use tools to build coalitions on these and other wedge issues. For instance, they supply messages that boost working-class support for universal childcare by nearly 28 points, climate change action by nearly 24 points, supporting trans girls on sports teams by 23 points, citizenship paths for immigrants by 22 points.Their findings indicate that the working-class is not rabidly pro–Immigration and Customs Enforcement or militantly against civil liberties, and a coalition that favors immigrant safety is not only possible but easy to communicate, even in the face of a right-leaning opposition actively seeking to prevent coalition.The report shows how the Right pierces a progressive cause’s flank when the Left assumes consensus. Progressives and leftists need to see past our bubble and realize that not everybody is at our elevation on subjects like climate and culture wars, and that when we assume in this fashion, we make asses of ourselves to the people to whom we preach solidarity.

articles.title: For Socialists, Legislative Hardball Has Limits
articles.author: Paul Heideman
articles.content: The Right, as Corey Robin has famously argued, learns from the Left. Edmund Burke argued conservatives should copy the Jacobins. The slaveholders, even as they denounced the rights of man, celebrated the demotic virtues of widespread slaveholding in the antebellum South. Newt Gingrich argued that the conservative minority in the House needed to adopt “Viet Cong” tactics to harry the majority. More recently, the Left has also attempted to learn from the Right. Liberal activists created the State Innovation Exchange (SIX) as a left-leaning version of the conservative American Legislative Exchange Council (ALEC). Further left, socialists have argued recently that the left should copy the parliamentary tactics of the congressional far right. Much of this discussion has focused on the House Freedom Caucus (HFC), the right-wing caucus founded in 2015. All the way back in 2018, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez herself contrasted the unity of the HFC with the much bigger but more loosely organized Congressional Progressive Caucus. In 2020–21, the “force the vote” debate on the Left centered around whether socialists in Congress should, like the HFC, threaten to vote against their party’s Speaker candidate (in this case Nancy Pelosi) unless they received a promise that one of their key legislative priorities (Medicare for All) would be brought to the floor for a vote. More recently, Neal Meyer has argued that the HFC’s success in bullying Kevin McCarthy provides a model for the kind of combativity and cohesion that we should expect from socialist legislators. I’m not convinced. In my view, the HFC has been considerably less successful than is generally appreciated, and the costs of its strategy have largely been ignored. Its example for socialist legislators is, therefore, largely (but not entirely) a negative one. Rise of the Freedom Caucus Before getting into the comparison, it’s worth establishing what exactly the House Freedom Caucus is. The caucus was founded in January 2015. The impetus for its founding was the failure of far-right Congressmember Mick Mulvaney to win leadership of the Republican Study Committee (RSC). Founded by New Right impresario Paul Weyrich in the 1970s to pull the party right, by the 1990s the RSC had become a central Republican leadership institution in the House. During Barack Obama’s administration, frustration with the RSC had mounted among the most conservative House Republicans, as the committee tended to support Speaker John Boehner in cutting budgetary compromises with the Obama administration rather than shutting the government down. When Mulvaney lost the RSC leadership contest to Texas energy executive Bill Flores, he and his ideological confreres determined that a new organization was needed for conservatives unwilling to compromise with liberalism. While the RSC leadership vote was the proximal cause, the founders of the HFC were also reacting against the failure of the House Tea Party Caucus. This caucus had been founded in July 2010 as the organization of the new belligerent right that was then storming Republican primaries. But despite the attention the caucus and its members commanded, by summer 2012 the organization was defunct, having failed, as an organization, to have much influence on anything. Mulvaney and his comrades, notably Jim Jordan of Ohio and Raul Labrador of Idaho, were determined to avoid a repeat of the Tea Party Caucus. Instead of a group that was publicity-seeking and undisciplined, they wanted a group that would be secretive and highly coordinated. To that end, they shut out House members like Louie Gohmert and Thomas Massie, who, while deeply conservative, had reputations as undisciplined loose cannons. The new caucus would be invitation-only and, unlike most caucuses, would not make its membership public. It would also bind its members by rules like the 80 percent threshold, which held that if 80 percent of the caucus supported a vote, the remaining 20 percent would have to follow. Very quickly, the caucus became a thorn in Speaker John Boehner’s side, denouncing him and voting against bills like Department of Homeland Security (DHS) funding and trade deal authority for the president. Boehner used his power as Speaker to retaliate, removing HFC members from subcommittees and cutting some off from National Republican Congressional Committee funds. In July, Mark Meadows filed a motion to vacate the chair, calling for a vote on Boehner’s speakership in the middle of the term. It was an extraordinary move, the first such motion in nearly a century. In order to avoid a bruising leadership fight that might end in defeat anyways, Boehner announced his retirement. He was replaced by Paul Ryan. In the 2016 presidential race, the HFC didn’t play much of a role. The group was opposed to Trump, who it correctly saw as totally uncommitted to fiscal conservatism. It was largely divided between Ted Cruz, who had built a strong connection with the HFC, and Rand Paul, whose dogmatic libertarianism appealed to several of the group’s leaders. Though discipline and unity had been the caucus’s founding watchwords, it did not attempt to make a coordinated intervention into the Republican primary. The House Freedom Caucus and Trump When Donald Trump became president, the posture of the group shifted considerably. While it continued pushing for far-right priorities, it did not engage in the kind of all-out warfare it had directed against Boehner. Instead, the group often compromised, and when it did fight, it often lost. On taxes, perhaps the cause closest to the caucus’s heart, there were two priorities in 2017. First, it wanted Trump’s tax cut to be deficit-neutral so it wouldn’t increase the deficit. In this, it was in accordance with the House leadership. Paul Ryan wanted the same thing. But it was opposed to Ryan’s means of paying for it — a border adjustment tax (BAT) that would amount to a huge tax increase on importers. This formed its second priority. Ryan would junk the BAT in summer 2017, though the HFC could hardly claim sole credit. The tax spurred opposition from a huge sector of business, from retailers to the Koch brothers, the latter of which used their connections with the Trump White House to turn the administration against the BAT as well. But with the BAT gone, there was no way to make the tax cut deficit-neutral without huge spending cuts that would derail the entire bill. The HFC pushed for these, but got nowhere, and the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act passed without any compensating spending cuts or new revenue. The second major fight for the HFC was Obamacare repeal. The caucus wanted a full repeal. Here the HFC did come into serious conflict with the Republican leadership and the Trump administration and was regularly denounced by both. Two members actually left the caucus in the midst of this battle. Paul Ryan had developed a bill, the American Health Care Act (AHCA), that would repeal much of Obamacare but left in place some of the original bill’s new taxes and also offered refundable tax credits to help households purchase health insurance. The HFC refused to support the bill, and lacking the votes to pass it, the House leadership canceled its scheduled vote on it. It subsequently passed amendments that would bring the bill closer in line with what the HFC wanted. Though it didn’t win all of its demands, the HFC agreed to support the bill. Mark Meadows explained that “had we not come around . . . there would have been the typical stereotype that they’ll never get to ‘yes.’” But even in compromising, the HFC was unable to achieve its demands. The revisions to the bill had made it too conservative for moderate Republicans, who pulled their support, dooming the AHCA once and for all. When the Democrats took back the House in 2018, the HFC faded in prominence. The reason is simple. To be a minority of a majority is to have some power. But to be a minority of a minority is simply to be powerless. From 2019–2023, the HFC voted basically the same as other Republicans. It joined the fight to defend Donald Trump against impeachment, causing one of its members, Justin Amash, to leave, and also worked to punish Liz Cheney for voting for impeachment after January 6. But neither of these distinguished the HFC from the bulk of House Republicans. When its party was in the minority, the caucus simply did not have very much power. Flexing Its Muscle? All of this changed after the GOP took the house back in 2022. As soon as the new Congress came in, the HFC was determined to exercise its power. Though the vote to confirm Kevin McCarthy, who had led the GOP conference since Paul Ryan’s retirement in 2019, would normally have been pro forma, it turned into a bitter struggle between the HFC and McCarthy’s allies. The caucus demanded McCarthy and the conference leadership take up various fights, such as impeaching Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas and creating a congressional subcommittee on the supposed persecution of January 6 rioters. McCarthy also agreed to give HFC members more committee assignments, to refrain from intervening in primaries without an incumbent, and, most consequentially, to bring back the motion to vacate the chair, which allows a single Republican to initiate a new election for Speaker. McCarthy’s speakership was hamstrung from the beginning by resistance from the HFC. As he attempted to pass budget bills that Joe Biden was willing to sign and hence avert a government shutdown, the HFC continually denounced him, demanding cuts that would make the bills unacceptable to Biden. As a result, in the spring and the fall McCarthy ended up passing more liberal budgets than he would have preferred, because he had to rely on Democratic votes to pass them. Though the HFC succeeded in weakening McCarthy, its actions made the actual policy outputs of this period more liberal. In October, the axe fell . HFC member Matt Gaetz filed the motion to vacate, and the House voted 216–210 to remove McCarthy. The race to replace McCarthy was messy. Four candidates tried and failed to win majorities. Mike Johnson, a fourth-term congressmember from Louisiana, finally succeeded after a chaotic three weeks. Though not a member of the HFC, Johnson had attended caucus meetings and received money from the group’s PAC. His election was widely viewed as a triumph for the caucus. Yet while Johnson was quite friendly to the HFC, for the remainder of Biden’s presidency, the group had little success in shaping policy. The Senate still held a slim Democratic majority, so any bill the House hoped to pass needed to be acceptable to Chuck Schumer. When Johnson pushed through appropriations bills that did little to advance HFC priorities, caucus members wailed and gnashed their teeth but could not change the legislation and would not try to remove Johnson over the betrayal. The Republicans’ victory in the 2024 elections returned the party to unified control over the federal government. The margin in the House, however, was quite small. As such, it might be expected that the HFC would yield disproportionate power in this environment. However, the reality has been rather different. As political scientist Frances Lee has shown , “During the first seven months of 2025, the HFC collapsed as a distinct voting bloc in the House Republican conference.” When Trump wanted to pass a continuing resolution that sustained spending levels appropriated under Biden, the HFC unanimously supported him, despite some complaint. Similarly, when Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill failed to include spending cuts savage enough to offset its tax cuts, the HFC released a document criticizing the bill, and five members voted against a rule to proceed. But when Johnson continued pushing it, the HFC folded and unanimously voted for the bill it had just described as “morally and fiscally bankrupt.” As the 2026 midterms approach, the situation of the HFC has deteriorated even further. Almost the entire leadership is leaving the House. In the statehouses, where local franchises of the HFC have been set up, it is losing ground. Wyoming had been its most successful state. The caucus had won majority control of the statehouse in 2024 and announced an ambitious legislative agenda. But after it failed to pass most of it, its reputation sank. In the primaries this week, the caucus lost thirteen members in the House and six in the Senate. To sum up, as of this writing, the future of the House Freedom Caucus is uncertain. It does not exist as a distinct voting bloc anymore, and its leaders are departing. If, as seems likely, the Democrats win control of the House in November, its power will be diminished even further, as it returns to the status of a minority of a minority. Lessons for the Left Where does all of this leave the argument that socialists in office should emulate the caucus’s practice of what Matthew Green has called “legislative hardball”? In my view, there are three things that stand out as particularly relevant from the experience of the HFC. First, the returns to legislative hardball are highest when the caucus is a minority of a majority and particularly when there is an opposite-party president. In these situations, the caucus could use its size and discipline to compel the House leadership to enter into fights with the administration that it otherwise would have avoided. These were also the situations in which the caucus succeeded in winning more power for itself in the form of committee apointments and so on. When the caucus was a minority of a minority, it was effectively powerless and indistinguishable from the rest of its party. When a party majority was combined with a same-party president, the caucus often made noise and complained about policies being made but was generally unsuccessful in shaping the policy outputs. Second, the caucus’s actions often resulted in policy moving the opposite direction from what it preferred. Its obstructionism led its party leadership to look for votes on the other side of the aisle in some circumstances. Since some compromises had to be made in order to attract these votes, the resulting legislation was more liberal than it would have been if the caucus had simply supported it. Recalcitrance can have real costs. Finally, the HFC’s accomplishments have fallen far short of its ambitions. HFC members hoped that its work would build the caucus into a kind of third party in American politics (effectively a right-wing version of the party surrogate model that is popular in the Democratic Socialists of America). This has plainly failed. The caucus has failed to sustain itself as an independent voice in Congress and is deteriorating institutionally as well. The very tactics that gave it its power are in large part responsible for this deterioration. The caucus gained a reputation as obstructionists and is unpopular with much of the rest of the party. There are a few implications for socialists in office. On the positive side, the conditions in which socialist legislative hardball are most likely to be successful are those in which the Democratic Party has a majority in Congress and an opposite-party president. This is the situation that will likely obtain after the midterms. Given that, I think it makes sense to look for some opportunities for the new socialist bloc in Congress to throw its weight around. However, it is worth saying that socialists in Congress do not have the kind of organizational coherence the HFC operated with. They do not have an official caucus or any institutional means of cooperating. Building this should be a priority. On the whole, however, I think the experience of the HFC should lead socialists to be cautious about legislative hardball as a general stance. The risks are very high. A socialist caucus that rejects legislation as not left-wing enough, only to lead the House leadership to look to pass it with Republican votes instead, is not accomplishing very much for the cause of socialism. And obstructionism within the party can actually isolate a caucus instead of winning a leading role for it. In other words, I’m afraid the lessons of the House Freedom Caucus for socialists are fairly limited. This is a pity, because the task in which socialist legislators are now engaged, as members of a party they do not lead, is a tremendously difficult one in which there are few models from which to learn. But the experience of the HFC does at least provide some guidance as to the risks of following its example.

articles.title: Your National Political Committee Newsletter — Taking Big Swings
articles.author: DSA National: NPC Dispatch and Newsletter
articles.content: Enjoy your August National Political Committee (NPC) newsletter! Our NPC is an elected 27-person body (including both YDSA Co-Chairs) which functions as the board of directors of DSA. This month, check out our Socialist Summit roundup, sign up for trainings, join our housing justice book club, and more! And to make sure you get our newsletters in your inbox, sign up here! Each one features action alerts, upcoming events, political education, and more. From the National Political Committee — Taking Big Swings August Growth and Development Trainings — and Sign Up for September Leadership Intensive Saturday 9/12–Sunday 9/13 National Political Education Commission Application Deadline Extended to Saturday 8/29 RSVP for Housing Justice Commission Abolish Rent Book Club Beginning Wednesday 9/16! Work for DSA — Application Deadlines Begin Sunday 8/30 Don’t Miss Out on Democratic Left! Sign up for Our Monthly Newsletter Welcome New DSA Organizing Committees From the National Political Committee — Taking Big Swings DSA’s hot socialist summer continues a powerful winning streak! Over the past month, Metro Detroit DSA helped score another big congressional primary win with Donavan McKinney ousting the millionaire incumbent Shri Thanedar, on track to become DSA’s 7th member in Congress by the end of this year — bringing Black representation back to the largest majority Black city in the country, and making Detroit the first U.S. city to be fully represented by democratic socialists in Congress, along with reelecting Rep. Rashida Tlaib. At the ballot box across the country, state and local candidates from Michigan, Minnesota, Connecticut, Vermont, and Washington, joined our spring victories from Oregon to Arizona to Georgia to New York. Even when we don’t reach our goal the first time, DSA members are taking big swings that change conversations and teach us valuable organizing lessons to keep leveling up our power. As a first time candidate in south Florida, Oliver Larkin got over a third of the vote in his bid for Congress. That’s because Broward DSA, along with comrades from Miami, Orlando, Tampa, Pinellas, and across the country, knocked on doors, phonebanked, and more to reach voters with Oliver’s message on affordability, working class democracy, and shifting resources from militarism to public goods for all. Just a year ago, it would have been unheard of for a democratic socialist to do as well as he did in south Florida, and especially in Miami. In Wisconsin, DSA chapters across the state threw down for Francesca Hong’s campaign for governor, and came within 4,000 votes of winning the primary in a major swing state — demonstrating a serious base to revive and expand on the past century’s legacy of Milwaukee sewer socialism today. DSA has even more serious work going on to build our power all over the place: DSA chapters and organizing committees are fighting water-hogging data centers across the country! As just one example, Central Mississippi DSA and their community organizing partners helped push the Jackson City Council to pass a moratorium on data centers. They join chapters from Seattle to Corpus Christi to New York in organizing to protect our communities from corporate polluters! DSA members are organizing for migrant rights against ICE and taking on the proliferation of Flock surveillance cameras that undermine our civil liberties, from Cleveland to Houston to Los Angeles. In San Francisco, DSA members are advancing a ballot measure for affordable housing. The measure would dedicate city taxes on properties worth over $10 million to housing purposes. In Wilmington, North Carolina, DSA members built and placed over 30 bus stop benches over the past year as a mutual aid project to improve city transit. The benches were recently ordered removed, prompting an outcry that raises expectations about the quality of public transit we all deserve! DSA membership continues to grow, with more than 120,000 members and almost 200 chapters nationwide! Earlier this month, we were grateful to meet so many members in Chicago at our DSA Socialist Summit. For the first time in many years, hundreds of members from across the country came together in an off-year between our national conventions to learn new skills and share lessons from their chapter work. The Summit brought us together learn how we can organize to win a better world by strengthening labor unions, abolishing ICE, ending the genocide in Gaza and freeing Palestine, transferring power and wealth from the elites to the working class, and electing socialists in droves! Mainstream media watched closely, trying to read the tea leaves about what our members are cooking up next to take on the political establishment. Check out some of the recent coverage from MS NOW , CNN , the New York Times and NYT video , and TIME magazine ! And what they’re finding is the kind of vibrant, dynamic member-led organization that is practicing democracy in a way the American political system hasn’t seen in our lifetimes. We finished off the summit with an introduction and rally for our updated Workers Deserve More program — check it out here! Meanwhile, members of Young Democratic Socialists of America (YDSA), our youth and student section, voted on proposals and elected their leadership for the next year at the annual Young Democratic Socialists of America (YDSA) Convention. If you’re a high school or college student, and you want to start a YDSA chapter at your campus this fall, sign up for the YDSA Fall Drive today! As we move into fall and the temperature drops, we have plenty of opportunities for cool socialist organizing! You can join us in person at the Socialism 2026 Conference in Chicago this Labor Day weekend to hear Hasan Piker and DSA organizers on our Workers Deserve More program, labor organizing, socialist history, and more. And on Thursday 9/10 at 8pm ET/7pm CT/6pm MT/5pm PT, join us online for End Times Fascism: A DSA Conversation with Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor! DSA is growing everywhere because we know a better world is possible — and we’re up against an increasingly apocalyptic, supremacist ideology of the far right, where billionaires justify making the world unlivable for their own profits and then trying to protect themselves from the fallout by bunkering borders, retreating to private islands, or rocketing off to Mars. Writers and activists Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor lay this out in their new book End Times Fascism and the Fight for the Living World, with research and analysis we can use to inform our big task: to build a mass movement that’s strong enough to cancel the apocalypse and win the future as a public good for all of us. As we grow and transform our communities across the country, we’re showing what a working class future can look like. Read on for more on how you can get involved today! Solidarity, Ashik Siddique and Megan Romer DSA National Co-Chairs August Growth and Development Trainings — and Sign Up for September Leadership Intensive Saturday 9/12–Sunday 9/13 DSA’s Growth and Development Committee helps keep our movement strong! Check out our upcoming trainings here. Our core curriculum spans topics from meeting facilitation to membership engagement. And are you interested in taking on a leadership role in your DSA chapter? Or are you already in a position of leadership, but looking to up your game? RSVP today for the September Leadership Intensive the weekend of Saturday 9/12–Sunday 9/13. National Political Education Commission Application Deadline Extended to Saturday 8/29 Join DSA’s National Political Education Commission by Saturday 8/29 to participate in our first general meeting and leadership elections! If you are a DSA member in good standing and are connected to education or scholarship either professionally or through organizing, you are eligible to join. Check out our application for more details! RSVP for Housing Justice Commission Abolish Rent Book Club Beginning Wednesday 9/16! Join DSA members and tenant organizers around the country for a nationwide reading of the new book Abolish Rent, written by two co-founders of the Los Angeles Tenants Union, Tracy Rosenthal and Leonardo Vilchis. You can purchase Abolish Rent from Haymarket Books here. DSA members can get a discount using code AbolishRent. Book club meetings will be every other week starting Wednesday 9/16 at 8pm ET/7pm CT/6pm MT/5pm PT. If you can make it, please come to all three meetings, and bring a friend! Work for DSA — Application Deadlines Begin Sunday 8/30 DSA is hiring! Please apply if you’re interested, or send to someone you know who has the right experience. Open positions include: Finance Director, application deadline Sunday 8/30 Press Coordinator, application deadline Friday 9/4 Regional Organizer, rolling application begins deadline Friday 9/4 You can find details on our Careers page here. Don’t Miss Out on Democratic Left! Sign up for Our Monthly Newsletter Democratic Left, DSA’s official news publication, has reached a new peak of readership and productivity. The 24 articles published in July attracted more than 80,000 pageviews. To make sure you never miss an article, sign up to receive our monthly newsletter! You’ll get a round-up of the previous month’s articles on the first Tuesday of each month. DSA members interested in writing for Democratic Left can use the pitch form here to submit article ideas. Welcome New DSA Organizing Committees Welcome new Organizing Committees! Let’s hear it for our comrades across the country! articles.title: DeFlock St Pete: Our New Campaign Against Flock Cameras & the Surveillance State in Pinellas County
articles.author: Pinellas DSA
articles.content: Pinellas DSA launched the 'DeFlock St. Pete' campaign on August 15th. Cape Coral, Florida. Lincoln, Nebraska. Toledo, Ohio. Decatur, Georgia. Minneapolis, Minnesota. These are just a handful of the municipalities in which vigilantes have taken action to cut down, unplug, set fire to, or otherwise disable the automated license plate reader (ALPR) cameras installed by Flock along roadsides across the US. The spontaneous vandalism of Flock cameras serves as anecdotal evidence of the widespread disdain for this fast-growing network of AI-enabled surveillance technology. But, what exactly do these cameras do? Flock cameras are marketed to local governments as a tool for public safety. But, what they really do is create a powerful surveillance network capable of recording where and when vehicles travel, with the goal being to build detailed records of people’s movements. That raises serious questions about the ability of law enforcement to track eople without meaningful oversight. It’s also left communities across the country to grapple with the rapid expansion of the technology, and to debate how best to fight back. Why Should Floridians Care About Flock Cameras? The Guardian reports that Flock cameras “scan license plates billions of times each month in about 6,000 communities in nearly every state in the US.” As Zach S., a PDSA member and one of the organizers helping launch our DeFlock St. Pete campaign explains: “These cameras scan the license plate of every passing car and feed this data into a database that can be used by law enforcement to track people’s locations without requiring a search warrant. They also use AI features to record other identifying features of cars like make, model, color, racks, etc. Flock data is also typically shared with thousands of other law enforcement agencies across the country through broad data sharing agreements. St. Pete started a pilot program in 2022 with 25 cameras, then extended this in 2024 with a $730,000, five-year contract for 50 cameras. This agreement was approved by city council on the consent agenda without any discussion or public input. Due to the limited transparency of St. Pete PD and difficulties acquiring public records, it is very hard to see how Flock is actually being used in the city or what sort of data sharing agreements are in place.” Did these mass surveillance cameras sprout with any meaningful democratic input from the people being surveilled? Of course not. Courts have long recognized that certain forms of location tracking require law enforcement to obtain a warrant. For example, courts have ruled that police generally cannot obtain cell phone location data or use GPS trackers to monitor someone’s movements without meeting constitutional requirements. Flock cameras raise concerns because they can enable a similar form of location tracking without any safeguards. By recording license plates and the locations and times at which vehicles are observed, networks of ALPR cameras can be used to reconstruct where someone has traveled and when. Anyone who drives through a neighborhood with a Flock camera can have their movements recorded. This isn’t just a civil liberties issue in the abstract; it carries frighteningly real and practical ramifications. Earlier this month, right here in the Tampa Bay area, Haines City Police officer Christopher Goodson was arrested for “misusing” a Flock camera database to stalk his former spouse. As Fox 13 reports , Goodson “logged 717 unauthorized inquiries into his estranged wife’s vehicle between September 2024 and June 2026.” “Our Fourth Amendment is supposed to protect us from unreasonable search,” Zach added. “Flock is subverting these protections and allows law enforcement to track anyone they want without a warrant. Since the courts are not protecting our Fourth Amendment right, we must take action at the local level to get rid of these cameras so they can not be abused. Until we do so, anyone could be the victim of the[se] abuses.” Flock Cameras are a Tool of Class & Racial Violence It shouldn’t go unremarked upon that, wherever these cameras are installed, they can — and will — be used as a tool of racialized class warfare by the ruling class against working people. “[Flock cameras] are being used to target immigrants, women accessing reproductive healthcare, and political dissidents,” Zach said. “Despite Flock’s claims that ICE is not accessing their data, independent reporting has found multiple times that this is not true. In Texas, a woman was tracked using Flock data for getting an abortion. There are many cases of law enforcement tracking protesters using Flock data.” The data sharing agreement is of particular concern when we remember the St. Petersburg Police Department still has a 287(g) agreement in place with ICE. This agreement effectively deputizes local officers to perform federal immigration enforcement functions, including issuing immigration detainers to hold individuals for ICE, as well as identifying, interrogating, and processing suspected non-citizens. Mayor Ken Welch and Police Chief Anthony Holloway have consistently claimed that the city’s 287(g) is just a formality and that local officers are not actively collaborating with ICE. But, where is our assurance that ICE is not being given access to data from the city’s dozens of Flock cameras? Every ALPR stands as an inherent threat to immigrant communities. Existing data on real-world use of Flock cameras backs this up. The Virginia Center for Investigative Journalism found that law enforcement conducted “nearly 3,000 searches related to immigration enforcement on Virginia’s Flock Safety network” in just a single 12-month period. The threat is not limited to immigrant communities. An analysis by Christopher Newport University found that majority-Black neighborhoods had four times as many Flock cameras installed compared to majority-white areas. Additional data from Oak Park, Illinois , revealed that 84% of drivers stopped in incidents tied to Flock data were Black, even though Black residents made up only 19% of the local population. All this shows that Flock cameras are not merely an issue of individual privacy. They are woven into the struggles for racial justice, health justice, international solidarity, and more. This is why, here in St. Petersburg, we’re organizing against the use of Flock cameras and demanding that our city put an end to its contract with the company through our new DeFlock St. Pete campaign. What are We Asking the City to do? Our demand is straightforward: remove the cameras. Cancel the city’s contract with Flock and do not replace it with another ALPR vendor. Dozens of cities and counties around the country have taken action to restrict or end their relationships with Flock. We believe St. Petersburg should join them. We understand that, in theory, there could be practical applications of ALPR technology. But, the broader question is whether we want to allow a system in which the government can continuously collect information about where ordinary people travel without any meaningful oversight or accountability. This is critical; if we fail to reject this level of surveillance overreach now, then it will be almost impossible to undo later. Our message to St. Pete city leaders: public safety and civil liberties are not mutually exclusive . We can protect our communities without creating infrastructure that can be used to surveil, over-police, terrorize, and abuse them. How Can You Get Involved? This campaign is just getting started, and building a successful movement will require educating and organizing people throughout our community. We’re planning presentations to local organizations, canvassing, social media outreach, and other public education efforts. We’ll also be reaching out to elected officials and candidates in St. Petersburg to discuss our concerns surrounding Flock cameras and ask where they stand on the issue. The interest from the community is there. The DeFlock St. Pete campaign kickoff event hosted at the Barack Obama Main Library on August 15th saw an overwhelming turnout; so much so, in fact, that more than two dozen people unfortunately had to be turned away due to capacity issues at the library. This shows that concerns about surveillance extend well beyond our organization, and plenty of ordinary Pinellas County residents are already onboard to #DeFlockStPete! Organizers have set up dedicated communication channels to help coordinate the campaign. Pinellas DSA members who want to get more involved in the campaign are welcome to join! More information will be available through Discord and, where appropriate, at meetings of our Socialists in Office Working Group. Flock cameras are already here. The question we now face is: do we allow an expansive surveillance infrastructure to become a permanent part of our community? Or, do we organize now to stop it? Get involved, talk to your neighbors, and help us demand a St. Petersburg where privacy and civil liberties are protected for everyone! Together, we will DeFlock St. Pete!

articles.title: If Woke 1 Was Crazy, MAGA Woke Is Absolutely Insane
articles.author: Branko Marcetic
articles.content: “Woke 1 was crazy.” Those four words, spoken on ABC’s This Week earlier this month by Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, unexpectedly blasted open the doors of political discourse. For nearly two weeks, debate has raged in columns and on social media about the concept of “Woke 1” — whether there was indeed such a discrete era, how bad it really was, whether the broader left is allowed to simply laugh off the “woke” excesses of the era. Or to take the opposite tack, whether trying to move on from those excesses is an appalling betrayal of activist movements. Part of the problem is that for every five people talking about this, you’re likely to get six different explanations of what “Woke 1” actually means. Here’s mine: it’s the tut-tutting, puritanical style of progressive behavior, incubated in and spread from college campuses, that believed you could yell, condemn, finger-wag, and cancel your way to political change — and that reached its fever pitch in mid-to-late 2020, when we saw a spree of job losses and censorship on dubious grounds, because people were being yelled at, or because someone above them feared they eventually would be. This was a distinctly unproductive response to the mass outrage and protest over years of unaccountability for police murders, which demanded serious changes to American policing but ended up in part being diverted into censorship and policing of people’s behavior. The “Woke 1” excesses people are complaining about now, the people hurt by them, and the absurdities involved, were very real: A business school professor removed from teaching his own course and investigated for using a Mandarin word that sounds like a slur in English. A data analyst accused of “anti-blackness” and fired for posting research about the impact of different protest tactics on the Democratic vote. A biracial makeup artist fired for singing along to a rap song that has a well-known racial epithet in the lyrics. A Mexican American worker fired after a white motorist hallucinated him doing a white supremacist hand signal. This was on top of the wave of censorship that saw scenes , episodes , and entire shows and movies removed from streaming services for racial insensitivity, even when satirical. Online mobs condemned Paw Patrol for its positive depiction of police, and thousands of Twitter users angrily piled on the late Barbara Ehrenreich after they misconstrued one of her tweets as racist. Not to mention, there was an undeniable overall cultural vibe, effectively capitalized on by the Right, of censoriousness that the vast majority of people found repellant. But all of this is a very long windup to say that it’s a bit silly we’re still debating the woke excesses of 2020 and earlier, when we are right now , as you read this, going through a period of objectively much worse and more dangerous woke excess, with none of the same scrutiny. No, it’s not “Woke 2,” or some new version of left-leaning cancel culture that’s erupted again. This time, it’s the people who describe themselves as part of the pro-Trump, MAGA movement who are doing the canceling and taking far, far more radical steps to do it than we saw six years ago. Call it MAGA Woke. The Sequel Is Always Worse There are so many recent examples that it’s difficult to know where to begin. Remember when Trump and co. just searched a glossary of vaguely left-ish words — including “history,” “culture,” and “ climate ” — and then just mindlessly cancelled whichever grant or contract came up in the results, even if it screwed over their own voters? In the process of enforcing their own particular brand of political correctness, Donald Trump and the GOP defunded everything from research into diseases contracted by firefighters on September 11 and cancer studies , to Holocaust-related history projects and programs for disabled teens — all simply because they used words that made them uncomfortable. This was on top of scores of government workers placed on creepy public watch lists run by right-wing groups linked to the White House for the crime of having political opinions that offend the MAGA movement. At least half of those workers were forced on leave or ended up leaving their jobs. Nothing like any of this happened under what Trumpworld calls the “woke and weaponized” government run by Joe Biden. In fact, the big, bad, woke, cancel-culture scandal under that administration was that Twitter, both under government pressure but sometimes of its own accord, throttled the reach of some conservative accounts — a serious matter, but one that doesn’t nearly rise to the intensity and scale of the speech-related repression we’ve seen since Trump took office. Speaking of which, that tech censorship of Bad Opinions hasn’t stopped under Trump, even though he won promising to end censorship and signed an executive order supposedly doing just that. The only difference between the old regime and the new one is the targets: instead of anti-vaccine posts, social media censors now target abortion-pill providers, pro-Palestinian advocacy, anti-CEO comments, pro-LGBTQ posts, and more. In fact, MAGA has expanded its woke weaponization of social media beyond the digital realm, revoking people’s visas, denying them entry into the United States, pulling their travel privileges, and more because of posts and memes critical of Trump, his allies, or US policy. Worse by the Numbers This is all anecdotal, you might retort. But MAGA cancel culture isn’t worse because it feels like it is. We know it is, by the numbers. After the murder of right-wing influencer Charlie Kirk last year, Trump, his Vice President J. D. Vance, and their allies went on a cancel culture crusade, publicly demanding the heads of anyone daring to make utter a critical word about the late commentator — a speech stricture, by the way, that they themselves regularly violate. The result? More than six hundred Americans were fired, suspended, investigated, or otherwise disciplined by their bosses for saying things that triggered the White House and MAGA world, according to a review by Reuters, the majority of them educators, including fifty academics and top administrators at universities. Compare that to the twenty-two academics who lost their jobs in the “Woke 1” frenzy of 2020 and the 160 people fired for their pro-Palestinian advocacy over 2024 during the start of what we might call the “Watermelon Scare” — the ongoing and yearslong hysteria around, and resulting repression of, advocacy for Palestinian rights. Nor did those episodes see the threat of state power mobilized to try to get a comedian thrown off the air for personally offending a left-leaning politician, but this is exactly what happened after Kirk’s death, after Trump was angered by a joke late-night comedian Jimmy Kimmel made. That intimidation effort against broadcast news networks is still ongoing , by the way. In other words, not only is “Woke 1” objectively not as bad as “MAGA woke,” it doesn’t even come close. In a separate Reuters analysis , the outlet found that the Trump administration was slapped down by federal judges — ten of them appointed by Republicans — in a whopping seventy-five First Amendment cases in his term so far, out of a total of ninety-three. By contrast, over the “woke and weaponized” Biden administration’s entire four years, federal judges weighed in on twenty-seven First Amendment challenges to its policies — a fraction of what Trump’s already racked up — and ruled against it in thirteen of those, or less than half, compared to Trump’s rate of 81 percent. Speaking of the Watermelon Scare, the crackdown on criticism of Israeli policy and defense of Palestinian justice is worse than ever under Trump. It turns out, somewhat bizarrely, that it’s criticism of the foreign country of Israel that is the most sensitive spot for the nominally America First movement. Donald Trump’s forces have arrested, locked up, and tried to deport, often successfully, hundreds of students merely for saying things that the MAGA movement finds offensive — specifically, criticism of Israel. It revoked one pro-Palestinian activist’s green card explicitly for criticizing Israel and is still trying to deport him today. Another activist had her visa revoked for cowriting an op-ed in her college newspaper criticizing the university’s response to the genocide in Gaza. They are just two of many. This has been condemned as dangerous and un-American across the board, by both the typically more left-leaning American Civil Liberties Union and the more right-leaning Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression . Both Trump’s administration and the MAGA movement behind him regularly conflate antisemitism with criticism of Israel — a conflation that is itself, by their own definition (“Holding Jews collectively responsible for actions of the state of Israel”), antisemitic. Using this dubious and offensive idea, Trump’s people have strong-armed universities into carrying out heavy-handed policing of what their students and faculty say, all in the name of protecting Jews on campus — by which they actually mean pro-Israel activists — from being offended. We know this is what they really mean, because it is Jews themselves who have often been targeted in this crusade, a form of pro-Israel cancel culture masquerading as a campaign against antisemitism. In fact, a whistleblower complaint just this week from within the Department of Justice laid out how much of this was driven not by actual concern about antisemitism but by MAGA world’s determination to cancel people for their pro-Palestinian speech. DOJ attorneys were, for instance, ordered to open an investigation into Columbia University based on a single New York Post article that detailed how protesters said and carried pro-Palestinian slogans and items. In another instance, investigators were ordered to do interviews with Middle East studies professors, Muslim ones in particular, at Brown University who had been accused of nothing, in order to trap them into saying something they could then call problematic. All of this has led to an unusual situation where — in the words of the Forward , a pro-Israel, Jewish publication — the Trump administration has both “sought to ban diversity measures meant to benefit minority groups, while in several cases requiring universities to create new policies to benefit Jews.” This is at the same time that cheerleaders for Trump’s cancel culture policies speak in language indistinguishable from “woke” progressive college students — like billionaire Bill Ackman, who complained about “how aggressive, intimidating, and disruptive [protests against the war in Gaza] could be to Jewish and Israeli students” and that “racism against white people has become considered acceptable by many.” This form of MAGA wokeness hasn’t just negatively impacted the Left. It has also boomeranged on Trump’s own movement, as when figures serving or appointed to serve in his administration were thrown out for their criticism of Israel, which a rival political faction within Trump’s movement cynically mislabeled as antisemitism. Ironically, several out-and-out antisemites continue to serve in prominent positions under Trump with none of the same objection from this faction — because just like with “Woke 1,” the exponents of MAGA Woke often use cynical accusations of bigotry as a way to litigate completely separate political disagreements. Let’s Have Some Perspective The excesses of “Woke 1” were very real and unhelpful, which the Left has to acknowledge if it wants to be able to move on from that period. But it doesn’t hold a candle to the frenzy of MAGA-driven wokeness that we are in the middle of right now, where it’s not just the private sector bringing the hammer down on workers who offend Trump and his movement but where the far-reaching use of state power is punishing and even criminalizing people for speech that MAGA figures regard as politically incorrect. Those efforts have seen people locked up, fired, doxed, exiled from the country, and even criminally prosecuted for their speech. This is all objectively worse than anything that happened in 2020–21. It would be good if, in between obsessing over dumb, years-old tweets about Thanksgiving and whiteness, the media grilled Trump-backed candidates about some of it.
